full_judgment: 5. Mr. Abu Nayeem with Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed the learned Advocates appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submit that the plaintiff of the present suit cannot be termed as trespasser in the suit-premises as his consistent claim is that he purchased the suit-premises in his possession from the real owner and he has valid right, title and possession in the same and he is or was never a tenant or sub-tenant in the suit-premises at all as alleged and that in the SCC suit the question of title could not be gone into and properly decided and hence he has instituted the present suit in the year 1987 before the decree in the SCC suit was passed and, as such, without final determination of the question of his title in the said suit, the plaintiff-respondent can be termed as a trespasser in the suit-premises and therefore the contention of the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant on this point cannot be accepted and the decision referred to in that connection by the learned Advocate for the appellant has no application to this case. Next, it is contended by the learned Advocate for the respondent that it is not disputed that the defendant-appellant has obtained a decree in the SCC suit for eviction of the defendants and for compensation and the same has been upheld by the highest court of the country but the law did not permit the SCC Judge to conclusively decide the question of title of the parties in the suit-premises which question was kept open for a decision of an appropriate civil Court and now the defendant of the SCC suit and plaintiff of the present suit has prayed for declaration of his title and confirmation of his possession in the suit-premises by his title suit which has already become ripe for final hearing and on the prayer of the plaintiff of this suit, there has been an order of status quo directed against both the parties in respect of the suit-premises but in spite of that, the decree-holder of the SCC suit, the present defendant-appellant, has been trying hard to proceed with the execution case for eviction of the present plaintiff and another from the suit-premises. In the above circumstances, the plaintiff however filed an application praying for temporary injunction restraining defendant-appellant from proceeding with the SCC execution case to prevent multiplicity of litigation and in the interest of justice and the learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both the sides was pleased to pass the impugned order of injunction against defendant-appellant for the ends of justice, presumably under section 151 of the CPC, though not specifically mentioned in the order. Mr. Nayeem emphatically contends that the impugned order is not an order passed under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the CPC in which case an injury as contemplated in rule 2 of the said Order must be proved before an order of temporary injunction is passed, but the case is different here. In fact, the relief of injunction was sought for under the inherent jurisdiction of the court and the same was accordingly granted for the ends of justice. Hence, the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant have no manner of application to the impugned order passed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection the learned Advocate further submits that under this section for prevention of the abuse of the process of court or for the ends of justice, the Court possesses inherent power to restrain any party from proceeding with the suit or proceeding pending in a different court provided the facts and circumstances of the case warrant exercise of such power. In support of his contention he has also relied on some decisions namely, AIR 1962 (SC) 527 (Monohar Lal Chopra vs. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hirelal), AIR 1961 Kerala 178 (Shama Amma vs. Venkappa Bhutta and ors), AIR 1955(Kundapanemi Ragh Vaiah and others vs. Inonva Lakshmina Royana and another), AIR 1950 Madras 219 (Ahmed Abdul Sukkor vs. Uallabhade, Kanji Firm). He further contends that staying any proceeding or granting any order of temporary injunction during the pendency of a suit or proceeding is a discretion of the Court concerned which of course has to be exercised judiciously and carefully and stay can be granted for a reasonable period for the suit to be disposed of. In support of his contentions, he has relied on the decisions in the case of Mannujan Begum vs. A Samad Mollah and others reported in 29 DLR (SC) 282 and in the case of Soleman Miah and others vs. lshaque Ali being dead his heirs and othen reported in 41 DLR (AD) 104. He has also relied on a decision in this connection in the case of A Barek Miah and others vs. ABM Serajul Islam reported in 20 DLR 501 to show that even if an application for temporary injunction is made under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, yet the court in the facts and circumstances of the case, for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of any process of the court, may however pass an order of injunction in exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It has been observed inter alia by their Lordships in the decision reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 527 as follows in para 18.
